content.title: Cross-task ensembles
content.review:
This paper suggests a method for producing diverse ensembles with meaningful uncertainty estimates by having each ensemble method use a different intermediate task from which to predict the output. The paper applies the method to dense-prediction problems for images, so each ensemble member first translates the image to some intermediate domain (like greyscale, or 2d edge maps) before predicting a per pixel laplacian distribution. Each model is trained in a supervised fashion with an NLL objective, and uses a perceptual loss to further refine it. To improve the uncertainty estimates under distribution shift, the model is trained in a 2nd stage to produce high uncertainty for distorted data. The final ensemble output for each pixel can either be produced using a trained mixture model or just using inverse variance mapping. Experiments show improved performance on corrupted inputs vs a number of baselines, both qualitatively and quantitatively.

Strengths:
+ I like the idea of auxiliary tasks being used to force networks to find diverse solutions
+ The results generally look good

Weaknesses:
- I'm totally unclear from the paper whether F_xy is a learned function or a procedurally applied transformation. There is no loss provided for it, but it is repeatedly referred to as "self-supervised." If it's just a procedurally applied transformation, it seems like it may be roughly equivalent to just using different data augmentation strategies for each model.
- The sigma training procedure is extremely similar to "Deep Anomaly Detection with Outlier Exposure" (Hendrycks, et al ICLR 2019). That should be cited at the very least. Furthermore, as that paper showed, as well as many others, training with specific out-of-distribution datasets to increase uncertainty does not generalize to all other forms of out-of-distribution samples. The fact that this paper always uses the same corruptions for this stage concerns me that they may have been handpicked with knowledge of the downstream task. I'd at least have liked to see cross-validation over the corruptions used for training and testing.
- I'm further concerned about using corruptions from ImageNet-C as part of the training procedure. ImageNet-C was released as just a test set and the paper says "networks should not be trained on these images." I recognize that what's being done here is applying their corruptions to a different dataset, and not literally using their dataset, but the point is that that these corruptions should not be used to train models to be more robust, since then we need a new set of corruptions to evaluate robustness against. It's good that you didn't evaluate on the same corruptions that you trained with, but these corruptions should not be used for training at all.
- The paper is framed as a general method for making predictions from neural networks that is robust to distribution shift. Since only one task is used throughout the paper, it's unclear how many of the contributions are generally applicable as opposed to specific to the domain of dense prediction from images(or some subset thereof). For example, is the Laplace prior generally applicable? Certainly the cross-task consistency loss is not. This needs to be discussed at a minimum and ideally also demonstrated experimentally. It seems like much of this could be directly used to train an ImageNet classification ensemble, for example.
- I'd like to see better ablations. How much of the improvement over DeepEnsembles comes from the separate Y domains, the Laplacian prior, the sigma training, the cross-task consistency loss, or the merging function? The baselines don't capture this, although the description of the baselines isn't clear enough to know in some cases. For example, is "Baseline UNET" also using the Laplacian prior, or is it Gaussian? What about the DeepEnsembles implementation?
- Are the architectures of each model (whether or not they are members of a larger ensemble) the same across the proposed models and the baselines?
- The "cross-task consistency loss" seems misleadingly named, since there doesn't seem to be anything cross-task about it. It seems to just be a perceptual loss (which also needs a citation - Johnson et al, ECCV2016) applied to each F_yz model independently. What am I missing?
- I can't tell from Section 3.3 whether Eq 4 was actually used, or whether the "alternative approach" of just using a standard perceptual loss on the predicted mean was used. If Eq 4 was used, how was g_jk instantiated?
- I find it really hard to understand what the overall training procedure is. It seems that there are at least 2 stages, where Eq 1 is optimized in stage 1 and Eq 2 is optimized in stage 2. When is Eq 3 optimized? Is there a 3rd stage? As mentioned above, I have no idea what version of cross-task consistency loss was actually used, but whatever it was, what stage was it in?
- None of the qualitative results are presented with groundtruth. That would make it much easier to evaluate quality.
- I don't understand what the different subcolumns of Table 1 mean. From what I can tell, the results are all over the place, with DeepEnsembles consistently winning the "Direct" subcolumns. The 2 "Ours" methods only seem to win a combined 50% of the time, but maybe I'm misunderstanding the table.

Minor details:
* In the Notations paragraph at the beginning of section 3, it says  the intersection of Z and Y does not equal the null set. Should that be "equals the null set?"
* The Training Details paragraph of section 4 references the "merging network." This term was never used before in the paper. I assume it's referring to the mixture weights discussed in section 3.2. It would be helpful to use consistent nomenclature. 

Reasons for score:
The general concept is good, but it is presented very poorly. It's not clear what is addressing the general problem of robustness to distribution shift vs just improving the single specific instantiation of the problem that is experimented with. The method is not clearly presented and is therefore hard to follow. There are also a number of important missed citations that make it seem like this work is claiming novelty that it doesn't have. A number of best practices are also violated here.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
We provide further clarifications of our proposed method and supportive results for its general applicability below.          


- _”corruptions … may have been handpicked with knowledge of the downstream task.”_: The sigma training stage **does not** affect the performance of the final predicted mean as it is forced to stay the same (see Eq. 2). Its objective is to expose the network to high distortions, which the original RGB images do not have, to encourage the network to output high sigmas. As suggested, we picked two additional distortion sets for the sigma training stage and evaluated the performance on the remaining unseen distortions. Performance is similar between the two new distortions sets and the set used in the paper (see Sup. Mat. Fig. 1), thus **any** high intensity distortion will do. 


- _“uncertainty does not generalize to all other forms of out-of-distribution samples“_: We now include adversarial shifts confirming that the method still outperforms the baselines and yields strong performance outside of the common corruptions benchmark (see Table 1). 


- _“it's unclear how many of the contributions are generally applicable“_: We added results for classification (see Table 2 for ImageNet-C, Sup. Mat. Table 1 for CIFAR-100-C and CIFAR-10-C) and adversarial shifts (see Table 1). Our strong performance against baselines suggests that the method is applicable to a wide set of problems.


- _“better ablations“_:  We now added ablation studies to show the impact of individual paths, sigma and consistency training, and the effect of each distortion on middle domains (see Fig. 7, Sup. Mat. Fig. 1, 2, 5, Table 2).


- _“similar to "Deep Anomaly Detection with Outlier Exposure””_: Thanks for the pointer, we have added it to Section 2 paragraph 5. The mentioned paper requires a separate dataset for calibrating uncertainties, furthermore, it is concerned with classification problems for detecting outliers using classification specific loss terms (e.g. margin ranking loss). In contrast, we do not need a new dataset for calibration and our focus is on obtaining robustness for dense prediction and regression problems. 


- _“concerned about using corruptions from ImageNet-C as part of the training procedure“_: We would like to point out the following papers that also used Gaussian data (part of ImageNet-C) during training and test on the common corruption benchmarks [3,4,5]. 


- _“is the Laplace prior generally applicable”_: A Laplace prior is typically used for the regression problems we have focused on [1,2].


- _“the description of the baselines isn't clear”_: All the baselines and deep ensemble components use the same UNet architecture and Laplacian prior for training, we made this clearer in the updated paper. 


- _“F__xy is a learned function or a procedurally applied transformation... roughly equivalent to just using different data augmentation strategies”_:  It is a procedurally applied transformation. In data augmentation, at test time, the input to the learned model is the RGB image, while in our case, it is the transformed RGB image e.g. 2D edges. Thus, each path is _forced_ to learn the mapping to the target from these middle domains. 


- _“cross-task consistency loss seems misleading”_: We agree that the consistency constraints can be considered as perceptual losses, we use the term cross-task consistency loss to refer to the losses used in [2]. We added the citation.


- _“overall training procedure”_: We added a table summarizing the training procedure to make this clearer.


- _“subcolumns of Table 1”_: “Direct” subcolumns show the $\ell_1$ error from RGB to the target domain (shown in bold). As demonstrated in [2], this error metric may not be able to capture fine-grained changes in the prediction. Thus, we computed the errors in several perceptual domains for each target to give a non-uniform attention to pixel properties. 


- _“methods only seem to win a combined 50% of the time”_: Our method variants yield similar performance to deep ensembles on in-distribution data, while being more robust against distribution shifts (see Fig 6, Table 1, Table 2). This demonstrates the robustness on out-of-distribution data did not come at the cost of degraded performance on in-distribution data. 


- _“qualitative results without GT”_: We have added GTs.



$$$$


[1] Kendall et al. “What Uncertainties Do We Need in Bayesian Deep Learning for Computer Vision?”, NeurIPS’17

[2] Zamir et al. “Robust Learning through Cross-Task Consistency”, CVPR’20

[3] Yin et al. “A Fourier Perspective on Model Robustness in Computer Vision”, NeurIPS’19

[4] Ford et al. “Adversarial Examples Are a Natural Consequence of Test Error in Noise”, ICML’19

[5] Rusak et al. “A simple way to make neural networks robust against diverse image corruptions”, ECCV’20

content.title: Official Review (Reviewer2)
content.review:
**Summary:** The work proposes a method that allows to build ensembles that are more robust to a dataset shift, comparing to conventional ensembles. The main idea of the proposed method is simple, but yet elegant; The (corrupted) input x is mapped to a set of middle representations (e.g., "wavelet, 2D edges, greyscale, and emboss"). Then, different models are used to predict the target of the original problem and uncertainty in the predictions based on the middle representations. The core hypothesis is that different corruptions affect middle representations with different strengths (e.g., color corruptions will have less influence on greyscale middle representation). The predictions then are aggregated based on uncertainties---the predictions that are based on less affected middle representations will be accounted for with higher weights. The empirical results are shown on depth estimation problem, the comparison with deep ensembles looks convincing.

**Highlight:** I want to highlight the especially interesting point that is demonstrated in the work. Many works in uncertainty estimations improve the ability of a model to estimate uncertainty in its predictions. However, it almost never goes beyond the estimate of uncertainty. Certain questions still remain unanswered: Are our uncertainties estimations adequate *? Are they adequate enough to be useful to improve predictions of the model? Is it possible to improve predictions based on uncertainty estimation at all? etc. Uncertainties rarely (if not newer) are used to improve the predictive performance of a model, that however is done in this paper, and I see it very interesting. 

'* the evaluation prosses is a weak point at the UE research.

**The major concerns**: 

The only concern I have is related to the area of applicability, and it is more like a question rather than a concern. 

The paper clearly demonstrates that the method makes the difference in depth estimation. Do you think the method will transfer to other problems (e.g., detection, classification, ...) and domains (e.g., sound, ...)? I certainly understand that it is impossible to pack everything into one paper, but at least I would like to hear some comments. 

Perhaps we are bounded to corruption where lack of certainty is the kind of obvious --- if the image is blurred then X transformation suffers and it is easy to notice (for instance via pure pixel-vise classification). But for example, if we see a completely sharp but out-of-domain object we may not recognize uncertainty at all.

**Minor comments:**

1. Use `\citep` for multi-citations \citep{work1, work2} and use `\citep` for (Boyd et al., 2004) style instead of manually adding redundant brackets like (Boyd et al., (2004)).

2. An unclear sentence "Similar to (Hafner et al. (2020)), we  ... "

3. There is a relation to test-time data augmentation [Ashukha2020, Kim2020].

4. Add colorbar(s) to uncertainties images (Figure 2, ...).

5. Maybe it worth to add some analysis like which corruptions break which transformations?   

[Ashukha2020] Ashukha A, Lyzhov A, Molchanov D, Vetrov D. Pitfalls of in-domain uncertainty estimation and ensembling in deep learning. ICLR, 2020.

[Kim2020] Kim I, Kim Y, Kim S. Learning Loss for Test-Time Augmentation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.11422. NeurIPS 2020.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and appreciation of our work. Below we address the concern about applicability to other domains/tasks. 


- _“transfer to other problems... and domains”_: We extended our method to the problem of classification (see Table 2 for ImageNet-C, Sup. Mat. Table 1 for CIFAR-100-C and CIFAR-10-C). The strong results show the value in using a diverse set of middle domains. On a different domain like speech recognition, frequency based transformations e.g. low pass filtering, can be potential middle domains. Our method provides a general framework, however, the choice of the middle domains depends on the data modality.


- _“bounded to corruption where lack of certainty is the kind of obvious”_: Good point. One obvious case of imperceptible changes is with adversarial attacks and we show that our method does outperform (see Table 1). It would be interesting to evaluate our framework on “natural” domain shifts e.g. dataset shifts like CocoDoom, CIFAR 10.1, ImageNet v2 etc. We leave this as future work.


- _“some analysis like which corruptions break which transformations”_: We added new experiments showing how each path is affected by different corruptions (see Sup. Mat. Fig. 5, Sup. Mat. Table 2).

display_title: Restricted novelty and setup combined with inconclusive experiments

content.title: Restricted novelty and setup combined with inconclusive experiments
content.review:
**Summary and contributions**:
- The authors propose a test time ensemble more robust to domain shifts in the input, by using multiple different intermediary domains, which reacts in a different way to the variations in the input distribution. They test over natural and synthetic datasets.
- The direct and 1hop pathways are combined using a weighted average ensemble, where weights are based on each pathway uncertainty. The uncertainty is learned, using synthetic corruptions for an input image. 
- The claims that the uncertainty generalizes over domain shifts and that this way the final ensemble improves the results under this problem are not experimentally proved. The differences between the baselines and the proposed method are minor.


**Strengths**:
- The work discusses a very relevant (mostly neglected) aspect in cross-tasks setups: the domain shift problems when using multiple tasks (learned or fine-tuned on different input distributions).

**Weaknesses**:
- The setup is very restricted, it is not proven that outside the common corruption set (on which the uncertainty is trained on), this will generalize over other domain shifts.
- The idea is very simple, mainly proposing an ensemble over a prior work X-TC (Zamir et al.), where the weights are learned based on a set of augmentations (sigma train). The authors train those uncertainty weights against some corruptions and afterward prove that their model is resilient to the same ones, on a different dataset, compared with methods that were not trained to understand those corruptions. 
- The results do not sustain the claims, but rather a very restricted task setup (to a common set of augmentations).
For all baselines (except for the “Blind Guess” one), the direct loss l1 (both on Taskonomy and Replica dataset) are almost the same, proving that even with a more general setup, the results wouldn’t have been conclusive.

**Quality**:
The method is not sound for the above-mentioned problems.

**Clarity**: 
The paper is hard to read. The ideas are not clearly expressed and the phrases seem rather hard to follow. The ideas could be more distilled, rephrased.

**Novelty**:
The novelty is very limited. The work is similar to X-TC from content organization, experiments, examples in the figures, to principles/ideas and conclusions point of view. [A] also shows an ensemble point of view in the cross-task formulation.

**Significance of this work**:
Very simple idea (to learn an uncertainty for guiding a weighted average ensemble), mostly using existing results from X-TC. The results are not convincing even for the given setup.

**Typos/Others**:
- Figures have very small/hard to read the text.
- Table 1 is hard to read (should have top1 entries bolded, or top3 entries colored)
- “Notations:” Z and Y intersection must not be void. Does this mean they should have common elements? I think this is a typo.
- ‘constraints”Zamir’ missing a space


[A] Semi-Supervised Learning for Multi-Task Scene Understanding by Neural Graph Consensus, Marius Leordeanu, Mihai Pirvu, Dragos Costea, Alina Marcu, Emil Slusanschi, Rahul Sukthankar

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4
content.comment:
We provide clarifications on our method and supportive results for its general applicability below. 


- _“prove that their model is resilient to the same ones”_: We use Gaussian noise and blur during training and evaluate on 11 **unseen** distortions. These Gaussian corruptions were used to train output sigmas only, not the mean predictions as it is forced to stay constant (see Eq. 2).


- _“with a more general setup, the results wouldn’t have been conclusive”_: Table 1 (now Sup. Mat. Table 3) results were evaluated on **undistorted** data which is **not** the main focus of the paper. We show consistent improvement in  performance against the baselines on dense regression tasks (see Fig 6), classification task (see Table 2, Sup. Mat. Table 1) and adversarial shifts (see Table 1). This shows that the performance of the method does not degrade on undistorted data, and it is more resilient to distribution shifts.  


- _“work is similar to X-TC”_: Our methodology and objective is clearly different. Our goal is to robustify the final prediction by merging the output of multiple prediction paths at the **test** time while X-TC uses consistency constraints during **training** to improve a network's prediction and does not have any consolidation mechanism. Our formulation and the training-time consistency constraints of X-TC are **complimentary**. We also thank the reviewer for pointing out paper [A] which has a similar objective with X-TC. We added the citation.

content.title: This paper is a little out of my area but it is well written and the technical contributions are clear.  I am not convinced by the final results as the performance seems to have a large variation in Figure 6 and the extra computation may not be worth the improved performance.
content.review:
The authors propose an ensemble approach to the problem of neural network predictions in distributions that differ from the training distribution.  The ensemble is combined via a principled manner based on model uncertainty.

The paper is generally well written and the approach is clear.  The problem of building robust models to differing application and training domains is important and well motivated.

Using ensemble methods to improve robustness is not new, but the methods of combining the predictions based on uncertainty estimates is interesting.

It would be interesting to see the approach extended to classification problems as well since changing viewpoints and lighting in application that differ from the training set can lead to poor classifications at times.

The error bars in Figure 6 suggest the performance of the proposed approach is not consistently better than deep ensembles or the other baselines.  Can the authors comment on this?  This may preclude the adoption of this approach.

The additional computation needed to alter the images and process the different paths would require the results to be significantly improved over previous approaches that require less computation.  It would be helpful if the computation speed compared to other models is provided, possible in fps.

It would be nice to see an ablation study showing different combinations of the pathways to have an understanding of the contributions made from each path to the final performance.

recommendation and reasoning

This paper is a little out of my area but it is well written and the technical contributions are clear.  I am not convinced by the final results as the performance seems to have a large variation in Figure 6 and the extra computation may not be worth the improved performance.
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3
content.comment:
We provide clarifications on our results, additional experiments on classification, and further analysis below. 



- _"proposed approach is not consistently better"_:   The original results were shown for 5 paths. A study on robustness vs number of paths shows that the outperformance of our method against deep ensembles is **monotonically increasing** (see Fig. 7a). The updated results in the paper uses 8 paths with clear improvements over the baselines (see Fig. 6). This is further supported by the perceptual error metrics evaluated under distortions (see Sup. Mat. Fig. 7).


- _“Approach extended to classification”_: We evaluated on ImageNet-C, CIFAR-100-C, and CIFAR-10-C and show that our method outperforms the baselines by only leveraging a diverse set of middle domains (see Table 2, Sup. Mat. Table 1). 


- _“computation needed to alter the images”_: Middle domains involve a few straightforward operations e.g. taking the mean for greyscale or two 2D convolutions for 2D edges. The increase in computation cost from going from RGB->middle domain->final domain is negligible compared to going from RGB->final domain as in deep ensembles.


- _“ablation study showing different combinations of the pathways”_: We added new experiments showing the contribution of each path in the final prediction (see Sup. Mat. Fig 5, Sup. Mat. Table 2).

content.title: Summary of revisions, arxiv link and project webpage
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their suggestions. We have updated the paper, the main additions are as follows:

1. Classification results on ImageNet-C and CIFAR-C.
2. Evaluations for adversarial robustness.
3. Ablation studies to understand the effect of each training stage, how different paths react to different corruptions, sensitivity to selected middle domains.

The paper can be found [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.10919) and project webpage [here](https://crossdomain-ensembles.epfl.ch/). 
Responses to the reviews below have been updated with figure and table references for the paper in the above link.
